extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; legislators and theorists interested in constitutions and citizenship
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative criteria for evaluating forms of government, magistracy, laws, and the nature/rights of citizenship as discussed in a classical political-theory text. Emphasises institutional design, selection and accountability of magistrates, property and population policy, and the civic virtues that constitute citizenship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of women's manners and property
rubrics_metrics.description: When the manners of the women are not well regulated ... it must not only occasion faults which are disgraceful to the state, but also increase the love of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim: women's conduct and property-holding affect public morals and economic distribution; a legislator should consider limiting or regulating women’s property (allowing none, little, or a regulated proportion) to prevent unequal wealth concentration and social consequences such as fewer citizens available for military service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of property distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: An equality of property conduces much to increase the number of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical standard: unequal division of land and property concentrates wealth, reduces numbers of full citizens (e.g., available soldiers), and undermines the common good. Laws that forbid sale but permit bequests/gifts may still produce similar unequal outcomes—legislators should design property rules that genuinely promote equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of pro-natalist incentives relative to economic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: To make them desirous of having large families he ordered that he who had three children should be excused the night-watch, and that he who had four should pay no taxes: though it is very evident, that while the land was divided in this manner, that if the people increased there must many of them be very poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion: population incentives must be aligned with land/property arrangements; rewards for large families can produce poverty if land is too concentrated—legislators should coordinate population policy with economic/land distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of high magistrates (ephori/kosmoi) from general populace
rubrics_metrics.description: These magistrates take cognisance of things of the last importance, and yet they are chosen out of the people in general; so that it often happens that a very poor person is elected to that office, who, from that circumstance, is easily bought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design principle: selecting powerful magistrates from the whole populace risks corruption if appointees lack means or character; selection procedures should aim to secure integrity and independence of office-holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written law and established custom as constraints on magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: They should not determine according to their own opinion, but by a written law or established custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance standard: magistrates with great power must be constrained by written law or established customary rules rather than arbitrary judgment to prevent tyranny and capricious decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and answerability of lifelong magistrates/senators
rubrics_metrics.description: It might be debated whether they should be continued judges for life ... there have been guilty both of bribery and partiality ... it had been much better if they had been made answerable for their conduct, which they are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability criterion: life tenure for judges/senators can be dangerous if members are corruptible; institutions should include mechanisms to hold lifelong magistrates accountable for misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid encouraging solicitation/ambition for offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor is it right for any one to solicit for a place he is desirous of; for every person, whether he chooses it or not, ought to execute any office he is fit for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: designing offices that only the ambitious will seek concentrates power among the over-ambitious/avaricious. Prefer systems where suitability and duty, not self-promotion, determine office-holding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of public meals at public expense to include the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: These should rather have been provided at the public expense, as at Crete ... so that all the men, women, and children were maintained from a common stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-policy criterion: communal provisioning (publicly funded public tables) fosters inclusion and strengthens the democratic part of government; requiring citizens to buy portions excludes the poor and undermines political cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating rival military commands that oppose central authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The commander of the fleet is in a manner set up in opposition to the kings, who are generals of the army for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security-institution principle: designing separate, potentially competing military commands can generate internal disputes and factionalism; command structures should be aligned to avoid institutional rivalry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutions oriented solely to war
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole constitution was calculated only for the business of war: it is indeed excellent to make them conquerors ... The destruction of it commenced with their victories: for they knew not how to be idle, or engage in any other employment than war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design warning: constitutions tailored only for military excellence neglect economic, cultural, and civil life, producing brittleness after victory; balanced civic and economic institutions are necessary for long-term stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudent public revenue and subsidy collection
rubrics_metrics.description: The public revenue was not well managed ... the state was poor, the individuals avaricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal standard: poor tax/subsidy systems that allow lax collection or unequal enforcement corrode public finances and moral character; legislators should ensure equitable and effective revenue mechanisms to support the state and discourage private avarice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of magistrates by merit rather than lineage or seniority
rubrics_metrics.description: Their method of appointing their kings is best, for they do not confine themselves to one family; nor do they permit the election to be at large, nor have they any regard to seniority; for if amongst the candidates there are any of greater merit than the rest, these they prefer to those who may be older.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meritocratic principle: prefer choosing officers based on demonstrated merit and fitness rather than birth or age to ensure competent governance and prevent hereditary decay of offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid electing magistrates solely on wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for those who are in bad circumstances to support the dignity of their office ... choosing men of fortune to be magistrates make a state incline to an oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection trade-off: selecting magistrates only from the wealthy risks oligarchic drift; the legislator must ensure that men of merit have sufficient leisure/resources to serve so that ability, not wealth, determines high office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not concentrate multiple offices in one person
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems also improper, that one person should execute several offices ... one business is best done by one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division-of-labour principle: avoid assigning multiple disparate offices to one person; specialization and wider participation promote better administration and popular support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election and tenure rules must be lawful and not at individual discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: They are also permitted to resign their office before their time is elapsed, and if all this was done by law it would be well, and not at the pleasure of the individuals, which is a bad rule to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional rule: resignations, removals, and selection procedures should be governed by stable law rather than ad hoc personal decisions to avoid instability and arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lawless force and factional revolts among the powerful
rubrics_metrics.description: General confusion which those who are in power introduce to impede the ordinary course of justice ... it is usual with the principal persons amongst them to collect together some of the common people and their friends, and then revolt and set up for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability criterion: prevent powerful actors from mobilizing mobs or private force to obstruct justice or seize power; constitutional protections and legal processes must check factional violence and usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a city as community of citizens with governance rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A city, in one word, is a collective body of such persons sufficient in themselves to all the purposes of life. ... there is nothing that more characterises a complete citizen than having a share in the judicial and executive part of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual standard: residency or mere legal privileges do not define full citizenship. The decisive mark is a right to participate in judicial/executive functions; use this functional test when assessing who is a citizen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office types distinguish citizenship rights (fixed vs indeterminate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some [offices] are fixed to a particular time ... others are not fixed, as a juryman's, and a member of the general assembly ... suppose we call it an indeterminate office: but I lay it down as a maxim, that those are citizens who could exercise it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic criterion: distinguish fixed-term magistracies from indeterminate offices (jury, assembly) when deciding who counts as a citizen; entitlement to exercise indeterminate public roles is central to full citizenship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancestry-based definitions of citizenship are problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: In common use they define a citizen to be one who is sprung from citizens on both sides ... it will be impossible to apply it to the first founders or first inhabitants of states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative note: genealogical definitions are circular and exclude founders and legitimate later incorporations; consider rights and functions rather than only ancestry when defining citizen status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of city identity depends on constitution/government form
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mode of government should alter, and become of another sort, it would seem a necessary consequence that the city is not the same ... when we speak of a city as being the same we refer to the government there established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ontological criterion: treat the identity of a political community as tied to its constitutional form; radical constitutional change may constitute a different 'city' even if population and place remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues of citizens must relate to the safety and ends of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one care common to them all, the safety of the community, for the community of the citizens composes the state; for which reason the virtue of a citizen has necessarily a reference to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative standard: virtues appropriate to good citizens are those that serve the common safety and purposes of the political community; civic virtue is not identical to private virtue but oriented toward communal ends.
